learner_notice: Commit one response before feedback appears. Entry checks are low stakes, and a missed fresh re-entry returns control without exit credit.

items.title: Starting check: infer an order from doubling
items.prompt: At constant [B], doubling [A] from 0.10 M to 0.20 M increases the initial rate from 2.0 to 8.0 μM/s. What is the order in A?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Guided practice: identify zero order
items.prompt: At constant [A], [B] triples while the initial rate remains 5.0 mM/min. What is the order in B?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Less help: assemble a rate law
items.prompt: A reaction is second order in A and first order in B. Which rate law matches?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: On your own: predict a combined factor
items.prompt: For rate = k[A][B]^2, [A] is tripled and [B] is halved. By what factor does rate change?
options: It rises by a factor of 6
It falls by a factor of 6
It rises by a factor of 12
It becomes 3/4 of its original value
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Near exit: infer two exponents
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Changed exit: derive the unit of k
items.prompt: A rate law is rate = k[A][B], and rate is measured in M/s. What unit must k have?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Repair: use one-variable comparisons
items.prompt: Why should initial-rate trials be compared in pairs where only one reactant concentration changes?
options: To isolate that reactant’s effect on rate
To make every reaction zero order
To replace measured rates with coefficients
To guarantee the rate constant equals one
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Fresh re-entry: infer a new rate law
items.prompt: Doubling [C] at constant [D] doubles rate. Doubling [D] at constant [C] leaves rate unchanged. Which law fits?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Repair: balance rate-law units
items.prompt: For an overall order n, which relation gives the concentration exponent in the unit of k when rate has units M/s?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Fresh re-entry: apply the unit rule
items.prompt: A reaction has rate = k[A]^2[B], with rate in M/s. What is the unit of k?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Starting check: predict k from temperature
items.prompt: For a reaction with fixed A and Ea, temperature increases from T1 to T2. What happens to k?
options: k decreases because T is larger
k is unchanged at every temperature
k increases as the negative exponent shrinks
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Guided practice: interpret the Arrhenius slope
items.prompt: A plot of ln k versus 1/T has slope −7200 K. Which relation identifies Ea?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Less help: compare temperature sensitivity
items.prompt: Two reactions have the same A. Reaction X has greater Ea than Reaction Y. Which is generally more temperature-sensitive?
options: Y because smaller Ea always changes more
X because larger Ea increases sensitivity
Both have identical k at every temperature
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: On your own: separate k from order
items.prompt: Temperature rises while reactant concentrations remain fixed. Which change is expected under Arrhenius behavior?
options: k rises while reaction orders stay fixed
Every reaction order increases by one
The pre-exponential factor must become zero
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Near exit: predict a controlled temperature change
items.prompt: A reaction is run at two temperatures with identical starting concentrations. The higher-temperature run is faster. Which explanation best fits?
options: The balanced equation acquired new coefficients
Reaction order changed only because temperature rose
Higher temperature raises k and barrier-crossing probability
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Changed exit: compare Arrhenius lines
items.prompt: On a plot of ln k versus 1/T, line P has slope −4000 K and line Q has slope −9000 K. Which statement is supported?
options: P has the larger Ea and steeper magnitude
Q has larger Ea from its steeper slope magnitude
Slope sign means Q speeds up as 1/T rises
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Repair: track the exponent sign
items.prompt: When T increases in exp(−Ea/RT), what happens to the exponent if Ea is fixed?
options: It loses the negative sign by definition
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Fresh re-entry: predict another heating effect
items.prompt: A reaction with positive Ea is heated from 290 K to 320 K with A unchanged. Which change is expected?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Repair: read the linearized equation
items.prompt: In ln k = ln A − (Ea/R)(1/T), which plotted variables produce a straight line?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Fresh re-entry: infer Ea from steepness
items.prompt: Two ln k versus 1/T lines have equal intercepts. Line M is more steeply negative than line N. Which barrier relation follows?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Starting check: identify the transition state
items.prompt: On a one-step reaction-energy profile, what does the highest point along the reaction coordinate represent?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Guided practice: calculate forward Ea
items.prompt: Reactants are at 15 kJ/mol and the transition state is at 65 kJ/mol. What is the forward activation energy?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Less help: calculate ΔH
items.prompt: Reactants lie at 40 kJ/mol and products at 10 kJ/mol. What is ΔH for the forward reaction?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: On your own: classify an energy profile
items.prompt: Products lie above reactants on the forward reaction-energy profile. Which statement is correct?
options: The forward reaction must be instantaneous
The catalyst has changed the products
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Near exit: identify the rate-determining step
items.prompt: A two-step profile has E1=10, TS1=55, intermediate=30, TS2=65, products=20 kJ/mol. Which step has the larger local activation barrier?
options: Step 2 because TS2 is the highest absolute point
Both steps because the peaks differ by 10
Neither step because products are above reactants
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Changed exit: infer reverse activation energy
items.prompt: A one-step profile has reactants at 20, transition state at 80, and products at 50 kJ/mol. What is the reverse activation energy?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Repair: measure each local barrier
items.prompt: For a multistep profile, from which level is a step’s activation energy measured?
options: From the final product to every peak
From zero energy to the tallest peak
From the preceding valley to that step’s next peak
From one peak directly to the next peak
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Fresh re-entry: compare new local barriers
items.prompt: A profile has reactants=5, TS1=45, intermediate=25, TS2=75. Which step is rate-determining by the profile?
options: Neither, because there is an intermediate
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Repair: separate Ea and ΔH
items.prompt: Which pair of subtractions is correct for a one-step forward profile?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Fresh re-entry: calculate both profile quantities
items.prompt: Reactants are at 30, transition state at 90, and products at 15 kJ/mol. Which pair is correct?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Starting check: identify a catalyst effect
items.prompt: Which quantity is directly lowered by a catalyst for a given reaction pathway?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Guided practice: predict equilibrium outcome
items.prompt: A catalyst is added to a reversible reaction already at equilibrium. What happens to the equilibrium composition?
options: Same composition; faster forward and reverse rates
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Less help: identify the kinetic product
items.prompt: Two products form from the same reactant. Product A has the lower activation barrier, while Product B has the lower final energy. Which is the kinetic product?
options: Product B because it is more stable
Product A because its pathway is faster
Both products because barriers never matter
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: On your own: identify the thermodynamic product
items.prompt: Product X forms over a lower barrier, but Product Y lies 25 kJ/mol lower in free energy. Which product is thermodynamically favored?
options: Product Y because its endpoint is more stable
Product X because it forms first
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Near exit: evaluate catalyst claims
items.prompt: A catalyst lowers forward Ea from 80 to 45 kJ/mol for R ⇌ P. Which additional change is expected at fixed temperature?
options: K increases because P becomes more stable
Only the forward reaction becomes faster
Both barriers fall while K stays fixed
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Changed exit: predict product control
items.prompt: Product K has the lower formation barrier; Product T is lower in energy. The reaction is reversible and held long enough to equilibrate. Which product is favored?
options: K because it always forms first
Neither because barriers and stability are unrelated
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Repair: separate path and endpoints
items.prompt: Which statement correctly separates catalyst and thermodynamic effects?
options: A catalyst lowers barriers, not endpoint energies
A catalyst lowers product energy but raises reactant energy
A catalyst changes K without changing rates
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Fresh re-entry: test a new catalyst claim
items.prompt: An enzyme accelerates U ⇌ V at fixed temperature. Which quantity remains unchanged?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Repair: distinguish the two product labels
items.prompt: Which pairing is correct?
options: Kinetic product → lowest endpoint energy; thermodynamic product → lowest barrier
Kinetic product → highest barrier; thermodynamic product → highest endpoint
Kinetic product → lower barrier; thermodynamic product → lower endpoint energy
Both labels mean the same property
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Fresh re-entry: apply short-time control
items.prompt: Product A has a much lower barrier than Product B, but B is more stable. Products are removed before interconversion. Which product forms more initially?
options: Product B because stability always controls first formation
Equal amounts because interconversion is absent
No product because equilibrium is not reached
Product A forms faster under short-time trapping
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Starting check: compare Q with K
items.prompt: For A ⇌ B, K = 4. Current concentrations give Q = [B]/[A] = 1. Which net direction is expected?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Guided practice: add a reactant
items.prompt: For X + Y ⇌ Z at equilibrium, extra X is added at fixed temperature. What is the immediate net response?
options: Shift left to make more X
Shift right to consume added X
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Less help: remove a product
items.prompt: For M ⇌ N at equilibrium, some N is removed while temperature is fixed. What happens?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: On your own: apply a volume change
items.prompt: For 2G(g) ⇌ H(g), volume is decreased at constant temperature. Which side is favored?
options: The left side with two gas moles
Neither side because gases ignore pressure
K changes to match the volume
The right side with fewer gas moles
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Near exit: predict an exothermic temperature shift
items.prompt: For R ⇌ P + heat, the system is at equilibrium and temperature is decreased. Which direction is favored?
options: Neither because temperature never affects K
Toward the side with more gas moles regardless of heat
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Changed exit: write a mass-action expression
items.prompt: For 2A(aq) + B(aq) ⇌ 3C(aq), which equilibrium expression is correct?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Repair: use the Q–K direction rule
items.prompt: Which direction rule is correct?
options: K changes until it equals Q
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Fresh re-entry: apply a new Q–K comparison
items.prompt: For U ⇌ V, K = 0.50 and the current Q = 2.0. What is the net direction?
options: No net direction because Q is positive
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Repair: distinguish shift from speed
items.prompt: What does adding a catalyst do to a system not yet at equilibrium?
options: Faster approach to the same equilibrium
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Fresh re-entry: test a pressure non-effect
items.prompt: For G(g) ⇌ H(g), both sides contain one gas mole. At fixed temperature, volume is decreased. What shift follows from gas-mole count alone?
options: No shift from equal gas-mole counts
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.
